newsitem.title: FRANCE: French UDF minister argues against franc fall.
newsitem.headline: French UDF minister argues against franc fall.

text.p: French Education Minister Francois Bayrou argued on Wednesday against any franc devaluation and accused those questioning its link with the mark of fomenting distrust of Germany to block greater European integration.
"We have no interest in a slide in the currency which would force us to raise interest rates," he said in an article in afternoon daily Le Monde.

Former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, like Bayrou a member of the UDF party which is a junior partner in the ruling coalition, called last week for a sharp franc depreciation against the dollar and said the franc was overvalued because of its link to the mark.

Bayrou said "It is enough to draw up a list of those declaring enthusiastic support for this proposal (devaluation) to see that it covers precisely those who fought against the European Union (Maastricht) treaty, from the right or the left."

He said "There is no automatic link between growth and devaluation." Italy and Spain, both of whose currencies had been devalued in recent years, had not shown any different growth than France. Britain, which allowed sterling to slide in 1992, owed its stronger growth more to the fact it followed the U.S. economic cycle, than the fall in its currency, he said.

"If the current value of the franc-mark link was so advantageous for Germany and so damaging for France, we ought to have a big trade deficit with our powerful neighbour. Instead we are very much in surplus, with more than eight billion francs."
He said Europe should push ahead in its drive towards a single currency, to arm itself with as strong a weapon as the dollar in battling for world trade.
"All currencies in the world are seeking the best balance between exchange rates and interest rates," said Bayrou.
The U.S. was the only country with a powerful enough currency to practice "monetary dumping" (dollar weakness) while still enjoying low interest rates.
Bayrou accused those questioning budgetary rigour, the franc-mark link or the Bank of France's cautious monetary policy of trying to create an anti-European and anti-German front.

"France's interests and Germany's interests do not conflict," he said. "French people must understand what the mark means for Germany, as a part of its national identity, and the dramatic experience Germans have had of inflation."
"It is not realistic, and shows no respect, to propose to Germany inflation and devaluation as a condition for the creation of the (single) currency," he said.
The Germans, in turn, must understand that for French people, the currency cannot just be left to bankers. "Europe is going through a time of very great fragility," he said.
"Those who do not want Europe are using every weapon possible to encourage distrust between Germany and France and threaten the project."
